summary: Despite hitting a plateau with Duolingo, I find its gamified approach engaging, but crave more practical speaking practice to truly conquer German.
top_quotes: Duolingo feels like a game where I'm collecting those wee gem thingies, but sometimes I forget I’m meant to be, you know, learning a language.
The most frustrating bit is when I finish a lesson and think, 'Right, Finn, you’ve done it,' but then ask for directions here in Berlin, and it’s like my brain switches off.
I’ve resorted to chatting up my local butcher in broken German just to get some real-life practice in – turns out, Bratwurst can be quite educational!

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Well, how's it going? Finn here, nice to chat with ya!

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it’s been a bit of a whirlwind, to be honest. Grew up in the charming emerald fields of Ireland, and after doing a bit of this and that, I found myself in Berlin a few years back. Wanted a change, something different, you know? I work in tech, of all things, and decided I'd have to tackle German if I was going to live here properly. So here I am, with Duolingo as me trusty sidekick, even if it's got a few quirks. It's been loads of learning, laughs, and the occasional ‘what am I doing?’

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in a small town in Ireland, a place where everyone knows everyone and the pubs are the heart of the community. It's the kind of spot where you can't walk down the street without hearing about your granny's new budgie.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was grand! Lots of craic, running through fields, and hanging about with friends. Everyone looked out for each other. I mean, sometimes it felt a bit like living in a fishbowl – everyone knew your business – but there was comfort in that too. It was safe, familiar, and kind of like being part of one big, occasionally nosy, family.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: Moving to Berlin was definitely a big one. I mean, that's a change and a half, right? I was getting a bit too comfy back in Ireland, and I just felt like, if I didn't do something bold, I'd never do it. Berlin offered a sort of new energy, a different pace. Plus, the whole 'speaking a new language' added an exciting, albeit terrifying, challenge. So I took off, bags packed and all, with a heart full of hope and a head full of basic German phrases.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: It forced me out of my comfort zone, for sure. When you're somewhere new, especially where the language isn't your own, you kind of see yourself in a different light. It's like, 'Alright, Finn, time to see what you're made of.' It made me more adaptable, more resourceful, and definitely more patient with myself. Plus, I've met some cracking people along the way, which has been a right bonus.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: There were times I felt like a fish out of water, but I leaned into the discomfort, if you know what I mean. I gave myself small goals – like tackling the U-Bahn system without panicking, or ordering dinner entirely in German. Made a game out of it. And, of course, Duolingo became a bit of an obsession for the vocabulary side of things. I hung out at local spots, picked up German through osmosis, and tried not to take myself too seriously when I flubbed a phrase. Humour helps, right?

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, it’s really about making Berlin feel even more like home and, of course, conquering this German language malarkey. I'm at this weird plateau with Duolingo, so I’m trying to break through that. I want to hold proper conversations without stuttering over every other word. And, I guess, I want to make sure I'm enjoying the journey, soaking up the Berlin culture, while also not losing sight of my roots back in Ireland. There’s a balance there, somewhere.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Well, it's kind of like solidifying this chapter of my life, you know? I reckon if you’re going to live somewhere, really live there, ya need to embrace the whole package – language, culture, the lot. Plus, being able to communicate properly opens up so many doors, both socially and for work. And there's something quite rewarding in not just existing in a place but becoming a part of it, if that makes sense.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day? Ah, that’d be one where I somehow swerve through work stress without breaking a sweat, get a solid German lesson in without wanting to throw my phone, and then just enjoy Berlin’s little moments – maybe a walk in Tiergarten or grabbing a pint with mates who’ve become family here. And if I manage to crack a joke in German that actually makes sense? Well, call it a win!

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: I suppose it's when I feel like I’ve ticked off all the boxes that mean something to me – you know, productivity, engagement, some learning, and a good dose of laughter. If I end the day not just having spoken loads of English, but a fair bit of German too, and still felt connected to folks back home, then that’s a good’un in my book.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: Ah, for the big ones, I like to mull it over a bit, weigh the pros and cons like. I’m a fan of the ‘sleep on it’ method, seeing how I feel in the morning with a brew in hand. I tend to chat with friends or family – they’ve a way of bringing perspective. And then there’s a touch of gut instinct involved. Sometimes you just know what’s right, even if it seems a bit mad. Like moving to Berlin, that was partly gut and partly wanting a good story to tell, you know?

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: I think I’d say I’m a bit of both, depending on the situation. I like having a rough idea of where I’m headed – some sense of direction – but I’m also open to taking the scenic route, if you catch my drift. Too much planning feels like wearing a straitjacket sometimes.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Right, so I had this weekend trip planned to Prague. Had my itinerary all sorted – places to see, food to eat. But then the train was delayed and threw it all off, naturally. Instead of panicking, I just rolled with it. Ended up wandering into a jazz club I never planned on visiting, and it was the highlight of the trip. So yeah, even the best-laid plans can benefit from serendipity.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I try to assess the risk first – am I risking a tenner or my peace of mind, you know? With big risks, like moving countries or switching jobs, I'll dig into the details, talk it out with people I trust. But if it feels worth it, sometimes you just have to take the plunge. Life’s too short to play it safe all the time, I reckon. Plus, most of the time, there’s less to lose than you’d think. You can always pivot.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it starts with a strong cup of tea, obviously. Then it's off to work, where I’m in tech, so a lot of screen time and problem-solving. I try to squeeze in a quick run or walk at lunch – clears the head. Evenings, I spend a bit of time on Duolingo or catching up with German news to get my language fix in. And if I can, I'll catch up with friends over a pint or a simple call back home to Ireland. A nice mix of routine with the odd splash of unpredictability.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, it’s the language learning that drains me the most these days. I mean, talking all day at work is one thing, but then switching to German requires a whole different part of your brain. Plus, there’s this mental push to not just coast on Duolingo but to actually use phrases in real conversations. Some days it's grand, and other times, I feel like I’m just muddling through.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I'd love more energy for diving deeper into German, honestly. I’ve got the basics down, but those intricate details – the grammar that makes you question your life choices – that’s where I need to spend more time. And maybe more time for creative pursuits. Used to dabble in music back in Ireland, and I miss it. Sometimes feel like I’m losing touch with that side of myself. Would love to jam a bit more, you know?

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Time's been a right bugger. Between work, trying to keep a social life, and learning German, the weeks just fly by before you even notice. It’s like, one moment you’re setting goals and the next you’re scrabbling to remember what they were. Plus, with family back in Ireland, sometimes I feel like I’m stretched a bit thin trying to be everywhere at once, if you know what I mean.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I’m trying to be more deliberate with my time. Made myself a bit of a schedule – nothing too rigid – but something that lays out priorities. And I’m learning to say ‘no’ more often, which is hard when you’re the type to want to do everything. Also, it's important to remind myself that not everything needs to be done in one go. There’s time; I just have to believe that sometimes.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: I'd say my family back in Ireland, for sure. We’re a tight-knit bunch. But I've also got a solid group of pals here in Berlin who’ve become like family. There’s Jake, my old college mate who ended up here too. And I’ve found kindred spirits in the oddest of places, like my local book club – who’d have thought?

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: Oh, they’re the kind where you can be yourself without any pretenses. With family, there’s history, memories, and all that shared madness. With friends here, it’s a shared adventure. We’ve all chosen this city for different reasons, and that bonds us in a unique way. We’re all in this big, messy, beautiful Berlin life together.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Probably at work, if we’re being honest. Otherwise, it’s at home in my wee flat or out exploring the city. I’ve made it a point to know my local spots – cafes and pubs – where I can unwind and feel part of the community. Feels important when you’re an expat.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Pretty comfortable, I'd say. My flat's a kind of oasis – it’s got bits that remind me of home, with my own touch of Berlin. When I'm out and about, I feel a part of the city. It’s this buzzing, electric vibe that you can’t quite replicate. And in the local spots, there’s a familiarity now – even if my order in German isn’t perfect, they know my face, and that makes it feel like home.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: I suppose it’s the connections, really. Whether it’s the familiar faces at the pub or the knowing nod from the barista who still corrects my pronunciation, it’s those little interactions that knit the fabric of daily life together. It’s both comforting and invigorating to belong somewhere.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: Ah, usually it’s my family first, even if it’s just for a vent over the phone. They’ve known me longest and seem to have an endless supply of advice, solicited or not. Then there's Jake here, who's basically the voice of reason when I’m losing the plot. And honestly, sometimes just talking it out with mates over a pint does wonders too. Everyone’s got a bit of wisdom to share.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: There was a time a few months back when I lost my job unexpectedly – just like that, poof, gone. It was a bit of a shock, really. There’s that moment of blind panic where you think, ‘What now?’ I’d just settled in, felt like things were finally on track when the rug got pulled out. Not knowing what comes next is, well, terrifying.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: Initially, it knocked the wind out of me. You start questioning everything – did you make the right choice moving here, what does this mean for the future? But once I took a breath, I saw it as a chance to reassess. It was like being given a reset button, scary but also kind of freeing in a way. You realize how resilient you can be when push comes to shove.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: Focused on the basics first: updating my CV, networking, reaching out to folks in the industry. I leaned a lot on friends, who were incredible. They offered leads, support, and more than a few ‘don’t give up’ pep talks. I also kept up with my routine – exercise, language learning, that sort of thing. Anchors in the chaos, you know? It helped that Berlin has a way of presenting new opportunities when you least expect.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: A bit of fresh air and a good walk usually does wonders. There’s a path by the canal here that’s become my go-to. Just me, some music, and the world feels a tad better by the end of it. And humor, can’t forget that. A good laugh somehow makes anything bearable. Can’t take life too seriously all the time.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I'd like to see myself more settled, maybe even fluent in German at long last. I’d hope to be doing work that feels meaningful, surrounded by good people, and continue exploring what this world has to offer. Maybe I’ll have found a sweet balance between my Irish roots and this adopted Berlin life. And who knows, maybe even thinking about putting down roots of my own somewhere.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I’d love to lessen the sense of being in a constant rush, you know? More time for creative pursuits, more energy for spontaneous adventures without feeling the pull of obligations all the time. And definitely want more confidence in speaking German. I don’t want language to be a barrier but a bridge.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was a bit of a hodgepodge, really. I’d picked up some language books, tried to listen in on podcasts, but it always felt a bit stagnant. Took a class once, but the timing never quite worked with my schedule. It felt like a lot of effort without much progress. I remember buying this hefty German dictionary – thought it would be the key – but it mostly collected dust. Couldn’t bring myself to tackle it after a day’s work.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: The sheer lack of structure, I suppose. I was like a ship without a rudder, just floating about with no real direction. Every time I sat down to study, it felt like starting from scratch. And the motivation just wasn’t there when you're not seeing progress. Plus, it was all so static – none of the interactivity or fun that keeps you coming back like with Duolingo.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: There was a particularly awkward moment when an old friend visited Berlin and I fancied impressing them with my shiny new language skills. But everything I’d ‘learned’ seemed to evaporate the moment I opened my mouth. Ended up gesturing like a mime, and my friend couldn’t stop laughing over it. That was a wake-up call that I needed something more engaging and consistent. A bit of a humbling experience, to be fair.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: Think it first came up in a conversation with a colleague over lunch. They were raving about how it made language learning feel like playing a game. I was skeptical but curious. So later that night, I thought, ‘Why not give it a whirl?’ and downloaded the app out of curiosity.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: Well, the whole 'gamified learning' concept was intriguing. Plus, it was free, and I’m not one to pass up an offer like that, ha! I liked the idea of fitting learning into little pockets of time, and the thought of not being bogged down by dusty old textbooks was pretty appealing. The owl mascot, Duo, was also strangely encouraging – felt like you had a wee companion on the journey.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Alright, so just the other evening, I sat down after dinner, opened the app, and got cracking. I usually start with whatever skill I’m weakest in – grammar, usually – those pesky cases trip me up every time. You tap into a lesson, and it's a mix of translating sentences, identifying pictures, or filling in the blank. Got asked to translate 'the cat is on the chair' – simple enough, but by the end of it, you're trying complex sentences and feeling like a champ if you get it right. I like the checkpoints where you kinda 'level up' – gives you a sense of progress. Ended with a listening exercise, which is always good to hear the language outside of my own voice. And then, of course, I collected my daily streak and earned a gem reward. It's all about those small wins, right?

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The repetition with variation, for sure. Like, you don’t just see a word once and forget about it. It keeps popping back up in different contexts. And the speaking exercises are a godsend – although I sometimes feel daft speaking into my phone, they’ve really helped with pronunciation. And then the leaderboard – it’s a wee push seeing where you stack up against others. For someone who's a tad competitive, it’s a good nudge.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, the way it sometimes feels like a guessing game, especially with the grammar. You think you’ve nailed it, and then you realize it’s all an illusion when you can’t string a live sentence together. And sometimes the app’s a bit picky – one missed umlaut, and it’s marked wrong! I mean, come on, give us a break, Duo! It’d be great if they had more real-life conversation practice, like talking with others learning German at the same level. That’s where the magic happens.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: Ah, it’s that plateau you get to after a while. You start with such a bang, feel like you’re flying through lessons, and then, wham, you’re stuck. You’ve gathered all the gems and crowns, but can you ask for directions without a stumble? Not quite. It’s like the app’s great for building a foundation, but where’s the bridge to real-world fluency? That leap can be daunting without additional support.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I remember it well. I’d been diligently using Duolingo for months, feeling quite chuffed with myself. Decided I’d show off a bit at this German meet-up by joining in the conversation. Let’s just say, it was like watching a toddler try to run. I was fumbling with basic phrases while others sped past. I went home that night feeling a bit deflated – it was a harsh reminder that Duolingo’s pace and real-life speed don’t always match up.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Absolutely. I try to mix in chatting with locals whenever I can – even if it’s just over a coffee order or at the butcher’s. Also doing German meet-ups or exchange events – those really push you out of your comfort zone. And sometimes I’ll watch German TV shows with subtitles, helps with the flow and rhythm of how people actually speak. It’s a bit like a language cocktail – Duolingo sets the base, and the rest adds the flavor.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: Real-life context, mainly. On the app, it’s all controlled and predictable, but conversations in the wild? They’re anything but! Plus, it’s more personable – you’re not just talking into the void, you’re participating in dialogue. You get instant feedback, which is massive. And it's more forgiving in a way – people are kind, eager to help, whereas the app’s just a bit more binary, you know?

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Probably that I’d give up entirely due to frustration and never get beyond this plateau. There’s a fair bit of pressure when you set goals for fluency, and not meeting them can feel like failure. Or worse, that my German would remain stilted and overly formal, never catching up to the nuances and slang that make the language what it is. I don’t want to be that guy who can only order a pint and not have a proper chat!

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I hope it gives me a good push in the right direction. Something fresh to tackle that day, keeps my brain engaged and learning. I want to feel like I’m making progress, even if it’s just a bit at a time. And I guess, a little reassurance that I’ve still got it, you know? It’s like having a wee cheerleader in my pocket.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: I reckon it’s when I find myself naturally reaching for a German word rather than my native tongue. Or when I can follow a snippet of conversation in the U-Bahn without feeling utterly lost. It’s the little triumphs that tell you it’s working – like when I realized I’d spent a whole day understanding most of what was said around me. That was a good feeling.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I’d love more speaking practice opportunities, like maybe pairing users to chat or some kind of interactive video lessons. The app’s brilliant in many ways, but it doesn’t quite mimic real-world exchanges. Having something where you negotiate meaning with another person would be ace.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: Just wish there was more integration between learning apps and everyday life. Like, linking Duolingo directly to other resources or events in your area – meet-ups or even online chats with locals. Make it more seamless so you aren’t just learning in a vacuum. Feels like we’re not far off, but there’s more innovation waiting to happen.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: Not much, just maybe that learning a language is a lot about persistence and patience, and less about perfection. We all make mistakes, and that’s part of the charm in trying. So cheers to still trying, right?

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: A digital twin, eh? Sounds intriguing, sure why not! Just don’t make him too perfect – gotta have some of the quirks and all!
